entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 2Co 4:1-18 . His Preaching Is Open and Sincere, though to Many the Gospel Is Hidden. For he preaches Christ, not himself: the human vessel is frail that God may have the glory; yet, though frail, faith and the hope of future glory sustain him amidst the decay of the outward man. 1. Therefore-- Greek, "For this cause": Because we have the liberty-giving Spirit of the Lord, and with unveiled face behold His glory ( 2Co 3:17 , 18 ). seeing we have this ministry-- "The ministration of the Spirit" ( 2Co 3:8 , 9 ): the ministry of such a spiritual, liberty-giving Gospel: resuming 2Co 3:6 , 8 . received mercy-- from God, in having had this ministry conferred on us ( 2Co 3:5 ). The sense of "mercy" received from God, makes men active for God ( 1Ti 1:11-13 ). we faint not-- in boldness of speech and action, and patience in suffering ( 2Co 4:2 , 8-16 , &c.).

He refers to the disingenuous artifices of "many" teachers at Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13-2Cor.11.15">11:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen34214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handling ... deceitfully--</hi>so "corrupt" or adulterate "the word of God" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.3">1Th 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen34215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commending--</hi>recommending ourselves: recurring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>.<div eID="gen34216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to--</hi>to the verdict of.<div eID="gen34217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every man's conscience--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2Co 5:11</reference>). In whom--</hi>Translate, "In whose case."<div eID="gen34224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">god of this world--</hi>The worldly make him their God (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). He is, in fact, "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that ruleth in the children of disobedience" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen34225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minds--</hi>"understandings": "mental perceptions," as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>.<div eID="gen34226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them which believe not--</hi>the same as "them that are lost" (or "are perishing"). Compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:10-12</reference>. South quaintly says, "when the malefactor's eyes are covered, he is not far from his execution" (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.8">Es 7:8</reference>). Those perishing unbelievers are not merely veiled, but blinded (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">15</reference>): Greek, not "blinded," but "hardened."<div eID="gen34227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light of the glorious gospel of Christ--</hi>Translate, "The illumination (enlightening: the propagation from those already enlightened, to others of the light) of the Gospel of the glory of Christ." "The glory of Christ" is not a mere quality (as "glorious" would express) of the Gospel; it is its very essence and subject matter.<div eID="gen34228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">image of God--</hi>implying identity of nature and essence (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). He who desires to see "the glory of God," may see it "in the face of Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14-1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:14-16</reference>). Paul here recurs to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>. Christ is "the image of God," into which "same image" we, looking on it in the mirror of the Gospel, are changed by the Spirit; but this image is not visible to those blinded by Satan [Alford]. <div eID="gen34229" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>proof that we are true servants of Jesus unto you.<div eID="gen34232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded the light--</hi>Greek, "By speaking the word, commanded light" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Ge 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen34233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath shined--</hi>rather, as Greek, "is He who shined." (It is God) who commanded light, &c., that shined, &c., (<reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference>): Himself our Light and Sun, as well as the Creator of light (Mal 4:2; <reference osisRef="John.8.12">Joh 8:12</reference>). The physical world answers to the spiritual.<div eID="gen34234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in our hearts--</hi>in themselves dark.<div eID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to give the light--</hi>that is, to propagate to others the light, &c., which is in us (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the glory of God--</hi>answering to "the glory of Christ" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the face of Jesus Christ--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts retain "Jesus." The only true and full manifestation of God's brightness and glory is "in the face of Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen34238" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17233"/><div sID="gen34239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17233"/>7. "Lest any should say, How then is it that we continue to enjoy such unspeakable glory in a mortal body? Paul replies, this very fact is one of the most marvellous proofs of God's power, that an earthen vessel could bear such splendor and keep such a treasure" [Chrysostom, Homilies, 8.496, A]. The treasure or "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God." The fragile "earthen vessel" is the body, the "outward man" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16">2Co 4:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>), liable to afflictions and death. So the light in Gideon's pitchers, the type (Jud 7:16-20, 22). The ancients often kept their treasures in jars or vessels of earthenware. "There are earthen vessels which yet may be clean; whereas a golden vessel may be filthy" [Bengel].<div eID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the excellency of the power, &c.--</hi>that the power of the ministry (the Holy Spirit), in respect to its surpassing "excellency," exhibited in winning souls (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">1Co 2:4</reference>) and in sustaining us ministers, might be ascribed solely to God, we being weak as earthen vessels. God often allows the vessel to be chipped and broken, that the excellency of the treasure contained, and of the power which that treasure has, may be all His (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.30">Joh 3:30</reference>).<div eID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may be of God ... not of us--</hi>rather, as Greek, "may be God's (may be seen and be thankfully [2Co 4:15] acknowledged to belong to God), and not (to come) from us." The power not merely comes from God, but belongs to Him continually, and is to be ascribed to him. <div eID="gen34241" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17236"/><div sID="gen34247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17236"/><hi type="bold">10. bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus--</hi>that is, having my body exposed to being put to death in the cause of Jesus (the oldest manuscripts omit "the Lord"), and having in it the marks of such sufferings, I thus bear about wheresoever I go, an image of the suffering Saviour in my own person (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2Co 1:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.31">1Co 15:31</reference>). Doubtless, Paul was exposed to more dangers than are recorded in Acts (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">11:26</reference>). The Greek for "the dying" is literally, "the being made a corpse," such Paul regarded his body, yet a corpse which shares in the life-giving power of Christ's resurrection, as it has shared in His dying and death.<div eID="gen34247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body--</hi>rather, "may be." The name "Jesus," by itself is often repeated here as Paul seems, amidst sufferings, peculiarly to have felt its sweetness. In <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference> the same words occur with the variation, "in our mortal flesh. The fact of a dying, corpse-like body being sustained amidst such trials, manifests that "the (resurrection) life also," as well as the dying, "of Jesus," exerts its power in us. I thus bear about in my own person an image of the risen and living, as well as of the suffering, Saviour. The "our" is added here to "body," though not in the beginning of the verse. "For the body is ours not so much in death, as in life" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34248" type="x-p"/>

[Chrysostom] (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.11">2Co 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.12">12</reference>). Compare "now for a season ... in heaviness" ( 1Pe 1:6 ). The contrast, however, between this and the "ETERNAL weight of glory" requires, I think, the translation, "Which is but for the present passing moment." So Wahl. "The lightness of affliction" (he does not express "burden" after "light"; the Greek is "the light of affliction") contrasts beautifully with the "weight of the glory." worketh-- rather, "worketh out." a far more exceeding and-- rather, "in a surpassing and still more surpassing manner" [Alford]; "more and more exceedingly" [Ellicott, Trench, and others]. Greek, "in excess and to excess." The glory exceeds beyond all measure the affliction.
